newsitem.title: RUSSIA: "Save Lenin's body" measure fails in parliament.
newsitem.headline: "Save Lenin's body" measure fails in parliament.

text.p: Russian deputies on Friday failed to pass a measure aimed at blocking the eventual reburial of Communist leader Vladimir Lenin's embalmed body, which lies in a mausoleum on Red Square 73 years after his death.

"In the name of workers we demand hands off the mausoleum, or otherwise we will call for workers and peasants to march on Moscow to defend the motherland and its sacred symbols!" said Communist deputy Vasily Shandybin defending the resolution.

The draft resolution "Prevent an Act of Vandalism!", which would have been a public appeal rather than law, fell 11 votes short of the 226 needed for passage in the communist-dominated State Duma lower chamber.

Communist deputies later complained that the electronic voting system failed to record five of their votes and called for a re-vote next week. "It's very suspicious that the voting system worked fine all day until we got to this measure," said Communist Viktor Ilyukhin.
Following Lenin's death in 1924, his wife Nadezhda Krupskaya mounted a vigorous campaign to have him buried in a modest way.

But as crowds from across the country came pouring into Moscow to see the leader of the communist revolution, his Kremlin successors saw they could maintain a powerful symbol by preserving the body for good.
Communists and their allies in the Duma view preserving Lenin's body as a matter of symbolic importance for Russia.
But their liberal opponents pointed out that the Communist party itself has led the way in removing bodies from the mausoleum by burying the embalmed Stalin in 1961, eight years after his death.
"Of course (President) Boris Yeltsin, a former party boss, would only be following the traditions of the party by burying Lenin," Sergei Popov of the liberal Yabloko faction said.
Yeltsin last week touched off the latest stage of the debate by mentioning a possible referendum on the issue.
Yeltsin said in 1993 he would bury Lenin within weeks. But he then backed off, apparently deciding not to use political capital on the explosive issue.
Yury Denisov-Nikolsky, one of Lenin's longtime embalmers, has said that the body itself is now undergoing a recleansing undertaken every year or year and a half to maintain the moisture of the skin.

During this time the body is immersed into a tub of chemical solution for a two months, lifted from the tub on a stretcher, cleansed of excess dripping liquid, and then redressed and put back on display, former embalmers have said.
The mausoleum is due to reopen to the public next week following the latest round of treatment to keep the 126-year-old body whole.
